description: I am really into space and Mars has always been fascinating, so I think I'll have a lot of fun with this challenge.
summary: ▎ For the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, I built Marswalk Planner, a map tool that future astronauts could use to plan a safe walk on Mars. It covers the boxwork ridges on the lower slopes of Mount Sharp, inside Gale Crater, using real NASA and USGS data. The map shows a safe, flat landing spot and three science stops. Each stop has a task, like sampling a ridge or a hollow, to learn how groundwater formed the boxwork. Astronauts can move their stops and set the steepest slope their suit can handle, and the tool finds the safest route around steep ground. It also shows Curiosity's latest position and the quickest path to reach it, so the rover can study the rocks they find. Because NASA's first priority is astronaut safety, the tool also shows the radiation dose for each walk.
details:
What it does

Marswalk Planner is an interactive map that helps an astronaut plan a safe walk on Mars. It covers a 2.4 km square of boxwork ridges on the lower slopes of Mount Sharp, inside Gale Crater. The astronaut sets the steepest slope their spacesuit can handle and moves three science stops. The tool then finds a safe, flat landing spot near the first stop, finds the safest walking route through the stops while avoiding ground that is too steep, shows Curiosity's latest position and the quickest path from each stop to the rover, and shows the radiation dose for the walk plus the temperature and the best time to walk. Everything updates right away when the astronaut changes something. A legend on the map explains every marker and color.

Science goal

The big question is how groundwater built the boxwork. Each stop has a task based on NASA's boxwork findings. Stop A samples the rock just before the ridges. Stop B follows the crack down a ridge top and samples it (Curiosity found clay minerals in a ridge). Stop C maps the nodules in a hollow and samples it (NASA cannot yet explain the nodules, and Curiosity found carbonate minerals in a hollow).

How it works

I used real NASA and USGS data: a photo map made from orbiter images (HiRISE, CTX, and HRSC), a 1 m height map of Gale Crater, Curiosity's path and position from NASA/JPL, Curiosity's Front Hazcam photos, and radiation and weather numbers from Curiosity's RAD and REMS instruments. A Python program reads a small piece of the USGS files and turns the height map into a slope map on a 4 m grid, about one suit step. The web page uses a path-finding method (A* search) that treats steeper ground as harder to walk and blocks ground steeper than the astronaut's limit. The landing search finds the closest flat area (under 8 degrees and 50 m wide) with no steep ground within 60 m. The radiation dose is Curiosity's surface average (0.67 mSv per day) times the walk time.

Benefits and impact

Today's Mars maps show whole regions, but a crew on foot needs the next few hundred meters. This tool combines photos, terrain, and safety data at walking size, so a crew can compare routes and know the risks before they go outside. The same method could work for any place on Mars that has a height map and a photo map.

Creativity

The astronaut is in control: moving a stop or changing the suit limit updates the landing spot, the route, and the paths to Curiosity instantly. The tool also plans a meeting with Curiosity, so the rover can study the rocks the crew finds.

Factors I considered

Safety came first, so slope is the main layer, the landing spot stays away from steep ground, and the radiation dose and the coldest time of day are shown. I also kept the design simple and clean so anyone can understand it quickly.

Limits

The slope grid is 4 m, so single boulders are not shown. The walk speed (1.5 km/h) and the suit slope limit are my guesses. The radiation and weather numbers are from 2012 and 2013 and are not live. Curiosity's position is a snapshot from NASA's data file dated November 13, 2026.

Tools

Python (rasterio, NumPy, and Pillow) to prepare the data. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the website, with no outside libraries. Netlify to host it. Keynote for the slides.

Use of AI

The code, the text, and the slides were made with help from Claude, an AI tool made by Anthropic. No images were made with AI. All map data and photos come from NASA and USGS.
